Test: `networkx_qa/ismags_map_nodes_s4_dataflow/files/testcase.py`, class `TestIsmagsMixedSearches`, its single test method `test_directed_and_undirected_searches` (pytest id `networkx_qa/ismags_map_nodes_s4_dataflow/files/testcase.py::TestIsmagsMixedSearches::test_directed_and_undirected_searches`).

Target function: the generator method `ISMAGS._map_nodes` defined in `networkx/algorithms/isomorphism/ismags.py` (dotted name `networkx.algorithms.isomorphism.ismags.ISMAGS._map_nodes`). Only the target's own frame counts; code executing in the frames of generator expressions or lambdas nested in it is attributed as described below, and no other function is analysed.

Tracked variables (local names of the target; nothing else is tracked): `candidate_sets`, `gn`, `gn2_cands`, `not_gn_nbrs`, `sge_color`, `sgn`, `sgn_in`, `sgn_out`, `to_be_mapped`.

Question: over ALL invocations of the target during this test method, which dynamic def-use pairs are observed for the tracked variables?

Definitions:
- Invocation = one call of the target creating a new generator frame (resuming a suspended generator after a `yield` is NOT a new invocation; the frame's state simply continues). Each invocation is analysed independently: a definition never reaches across invocations.
- Execution model: consider the chronological sequence of statement executions in the target's own frame. Each statement is identified by the absolute, 1-based line number (in `networkx/algorithms/isomorphism/ismags.py` as it exists in the repository) on which the statement begins; for compound statements (`if`/`elif`/`while`/`for`) this is the line of the header keyword, and the header comprises only the condition (or the `for` target and iterable), not the body. A multi-line statement or header is one statement executed once, attributed to its first line.
- Def: parameters (`self`, `sgn`, `candidate_sets`, `constraints`, `MONO_fits`, `to_be_mapped`) are defined at the line of the `def` keyword when an invocation starts. A statement defines a variable when it binds that name: plain assignment targets (including each name in a tuple-unpacking target) and augmented assignment targets. A `for` header defines its target variable each time it executes AND binds a new item (i.e. the next statement executed is in the loop body); the execution of the header that finds the iterator exhausted defines nothing. Item assignment/deletion such as `d[k] = v` or `del d[k]` is NOT a def of `d` (it is a use of `d`).
- Use: a statement execution uses every tracked variable whose name appears in a read (load) position anywhere in that statement's source text (for a compound statement: anywhere in its header), including inside generator expressions, set comprehensions and lambdas written in that statement (none of the tracked names is ever bound by such a nested construct, so these always read the target's variable). This is lexical: a read counts even if short-circuiting or an empty iterable means the subexpression is never evaluated at runtime. `for` headers count as using the names in their iterable expression on every execution of the header.
- Within one statement, all uses happen before any def. Augmented assignment (`x op= expr`) is both a use (of the reaching def) and a new def of `x` on that line.
- Pair: `(variable, def_line, use_line)` is observed when, at some execution of the statement at `use_line` that uses `variable`, the most recent def of `variable` in the same invocation was made at `def_line`.

Answer format: JSON object `{"observed_def_use_pairs": [...]}`, each element an object with exactly the keys `variable` (str, the bare variable name), `def_line` (int), `use_line` (int). Report each distinct triple once (deduplicated across all executions and invocations). Sort ascending by `variable` (plain string order), then `def_line`, then `use_line`.
